summary: Every book at Pennywhistle Books has a different swirl of color inside its cover, and tonight a traveling clockmender watches Willa Quince make one more by floating paint on thickened water, an old craft from Turkey called ebru. The rain taps the window, the papers dry on a line, and Willa dozes by the curtain.
source_tradition: Turkey and Central Asia (ebru, the traditional art of marbling paper on water)
source_note: Ebru paper marbling is a centuries-old, widely documented craft tradition; the shop, the characters and the story are entirely original.

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Tonight's story is The Water Paper, told by Tobias Vane, a traveling clockmender who happened to be passing through Fernwick. Get comfortable, settle into the softest seat you can find, and let the rain do the talking for a while.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Every Book Different]]

Mind the ladder, it rolls. There, you can have the bottom step, it is the driest seat in the shop. Now, I have been mending clocks in this part of the world for a good many years, and in every town I ask the same question of the bookshop. Why does every book at Pennywhistle Books open to a different swirl of color, and who makes them? Inside every cover, glued flat against the board, is a sheet of paper patterned like the surface of a pond at sunset. Not one of them matches another. I have looked, and I have a clockmender's eye for a repeating pattern. I stayed a whole week in Fernwick to find out the answer.

[pause]

Pennywhistle Books is a narrow, crowded shop on Harbor Lane, with shelves up to the ceiling and a rolling brass ladder that has never once rolled where anyone wanted it to. The owner is Willa Quince, a small woman with a gray plait and ink on her thumb. She cannot remember where she has put anything. She always finds it. Tonight it is raining, and the shop windows have gone soft and silver, and a lamp burns on the counter in a circle of yellow.

[pause]

The shop is full of small sounds, if you listen for them. A clock on the shelf by the door ticks at a slightly different speed from my own pocket watch, which I take personally. A bucket of wet umbrellas drips in the corner. The floorboards creak a little under the weight of the books, as a ship's boards do under the weight of the sea. And everywhere there is the smell: old paper, beeswax polish, strong tea, and the sweet, dusty perfume of ten thousand pages that have been waiting a long time to be opened.

[pause]

[[CHAPTER The Back Room]]

The answer is in the back room. Behind a curtain of faded green velvet, there is a long, low table with a shallow tin tray on it, about the size of a tea tray, filled with water. The water looks like ordinary water, but it is not. Willa stirs into it a pale gum, which makes it thick and silky, like the very beginning of a jelly, and she lets it sit for an hour until it is perfectly still. The air in the back room smells of damp paper, linseed and the faint sweetness of the gum.

[pause]

This is a very old craft, and it is not from here. It is called ebru, which is the Turkish word for it, and it comes from the lands of Central Asia and the old cities of Turkey, where artists have floated colors on water for over five hundred years. They drop paint onto the surface with a brush, and the paint does not sink. It floats on the thick water in small, bright rings, and the artist draws patterns in it with a stylus, or a comb, or even a single long hair. Then a sheet of paper is laid gently on top, and the picture lifts off in one piece, as if the water had been persuaded to give it away.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Willa and the Tray]]

Willa learned it from a woman called Selin, who came through Fernwick one wet October many years ago with a trunk of brushes, and who stayed three weeks because the ferry was late. Selin sat at this very table and showed her, patiently, with her sleeves rolled to the elbow. She said that the secret of ebru is to want nothing from the water. You let it show you what it is going to do. The thing you make is a conversation, and the water always has the last word.

[pause]

Selin had a way of making a person feel clever. When Willa's first drop of paint sank like a stone, Selin only nodded and said that the water was clearing its throat. When the second one spread into a wobbling, lopsided shape, she said it had personality. By the third week, Willa could drop a perfect circle every time, and Selin said that this was very good and a little bit of a shame, since the lopsided ones had been much more interesting.

[pause]

Tonight, Willa begins as she always does, by drying her hands carefully on her apron. The lamp over the table is turned low. Beside the tray are seven little jars of paint, each with a brush of its own: a deep blue, a rust red, a mustard yellow, a pale green, a soft plum, a cream, and a dark gray like wet slate. She picks up the blue first. The brush is made of horsehair, and when she taps it against a wooden rod, a single drop falls onto the water and spreads into a perfect, trembling circle.

[pause]

Then another, a red one, inside the blue. Then cream, then plum. The circles crowd one another and settle, ring within ring, until the surface looks like a pond in the rain. Outside, the real rain taps at the window glass, a light, steady patter, and Willa works in time with it, one drop to each tap. Her face is calm and slightly absent, the face of someone listening to a friend.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Comb]]

She takes up a long wooden stylus, a thin stick with a pin at the end, and draws it very slowly across the water. The circles stretch and curl. The blue follows the pin in a long, graceful swoop, with the red lagging a little behind it, as though shy. She draws it back the other way, and now the colors fold into small waves, like the feathers on a bird's wing. It is slow, silent work, and I will tell you honestly that it is the most restful thing I have ever watched a person do.

[pause]

There is a pattern she makes more than any other, and it has a lovely name. It is called gel-git, which means something like come and go, and it looks like a tide drawn in color. She pulls the stylus one way across the whole tray, and then back the other way a finger's width lower, and the colors swing out and in again in long, soft rows, like waves arriving and leaving on a flat beach. Tonight she makes it in blue and plum, and I could watch it until morning.

[pause]

At last she lifts a sheet of cream paper from the pile beside her. She holds it by two corners, bends it like a hammock, and lays the middle down first, then the edges, so that no bubble can hide beneath. For a moment, nothing happens. The paper rests on the water, damp and heavy, and then Willa raises it in one smooth movement and turns it over. The pattern is there, perfectly printed, with every curl and feather exactly as she drew it, and the colors are still glistening.

[pause]

She carries it to a line stretched across the room and pegs it up by a corner to dry. Dozens of other sheets already hang there, like a row of small flags, all different. This one is mostly deep blue, with red rivers in it. The one beside it is plum and cream, like a sky before snow. The water drips softly from the corners onto a folded cloth, one drop at a time.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Quiet Hour]]

So that is the answer, and it is a simple one. Willa makes one new sheet every evening that she is open, and the next day it goes inside the next book she sells. Nobody has ever asked her to. She says that a book ought to start with something nobody has seen before, even if only one person will ever open it. And she says that the water never repeats itself, so she cannot, even if she tried.

[pause]

She does not try. By now, the tray has settled, and the last streaks of color are drifting slowly together, blue into plum into gray. The rain has softened to a murmur. Willa dries her hands again, turns the lamp down to its lowest glow, and sits on the stool by the curtain with her hands resting in her lap. The back room is warm, and it smells of paper and tea, and the clock above the door says it is a quarter past something.

[pause]

Her eyes close, only for a moment, she would tell you. Her head tips gently forward. The line of drying papers stirs in a small draft, and the drops fall, soft and slow, onto the cloth below. I fetch a knitted shawl from the hook behind the door and lay it over her shoulders, and she does not wake. The tin tray holds the whole night in it, a quiet, swirling pond of blue and plum and gray.

[long pause]

Out in the shop, the lamp burns steadily on the counter. The shelves are still, and the ladder is, for once, exactly where it ought to be. Somewhere in the dark, a thousand books rest side by side, each with its own small sunset pasted inside the cover. The rain goes on, soft on the glass. I stay a while longer, and I do not mend anything at all.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Why does every book have a different swirl of color inside? Because Willa Quince makes one new sheet each evening.

[pause]

She stirs a pale gum into water. She drops blue, red and plum onto it. They float in small rings.

[long pause]

She draws a thin stick through the colors. They curl into waves. She lays a sheet of paper on the water, and lifts it, and the picture comes away.

[pause]

It hangs on the line to dry. The next book she sells will carry it.

[long pause]

Willa sits by the curtain. Her eyes close. The drops fall on the cloth. The rain goes on.

[long pause]

And that is the story of the water paper. The step is yours for as long as the rain lasts. The shop will keep. Good night.
